title: Miranda Rights - Right to Remain Silent
law_reference: Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966)
content: You have the right to remain silent. Anything you say can and will be used against you in a court of law. Police must inform you of this right before custodial interrogation. You are not required to answer questions beyond identifying yourself in states with stop-and-identify laws.
actionable_response: Say: 'I am invoking my right to remain silent. I want a lawyer.'

title: Miranda Rights - Right to Attorney
law_reference: Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966); Sixth Amendment
content: You have the right to an attorney. If you cannot afford an attorney, one will be appointed for you. Once you invoke your right to counsel, all questioning must stop until your attorney is present. Police cannot continue interrogating you after you clearly request a lawyer.
actionable_response: Say clearly: 'I want a lawyer. I will not answer questions without my lawyer present.'

title: 4th Amendment - Right Against Unreasonable Search
law_reference: Fourth Amendment, U.S. Constitution; Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968)
content: The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. Police generally need a warrant to search your home. For vehicles, they need probable cause or your consent. You have the right to refuse consent to a search. Refusing consent cannot be used as probable cause.
actionable_response: Say: 'I do not consent to this search.' Say it clearly and calmly, do not physically resist.

title: 4th Amendment - Vehicle Search Rules
law_reference: United States v. Ross, 456 U.S. 798 (1982); Collins v. Virginia (2018)
content: Police can search your vehicle without a warrant if they have probable cause to believe it contains evidence of a crime. However, you can still withhold consent. If police say they will get a warrant anyway, they must actually obtain one. A drug dog sniff outside a vehicle is not a search under the 4th Amendment.
actionable_response: Say: 'I do not consent to a search.' If they search anyway, do not resist — challenge it in court later.

title: 5th Amendment - Right Against Self-Incrimination
law_reference: Fifth Amendment, U.S. Constitution; Salinas v. Texas (2013)
content: You have the right not to be a witness against yourself. You must explicitly invoke this right by saying 'I invoke my Fifth Amendment right.' Simply staying silent without invoking the right may not be protected. This applies in all criminal proceedings including traffic stops if you believe your answer may incriminate you.
actionable_response: Say: 'I invoke my Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination and choose to remain silent.'

title: Immigration - Rights at Interior Checkpoints
law_reference: United States v. Martinez-Fuerte, 428 U.S. 543 (1976); 4th Amendment
content: At immigration checkpoints within 100 miles of the border, CBP agents can stop and ask about citizenship. You have the right to remain silent about your immigration status. You do not have to answer questions about where you were born or how you entered the US. You can say 'I am invoking my right to remain silent.'
actionable_response: Say: 'I am choosing to exercise my right to remain silent.' You may show ID if you have legal status but are not required to answer questions.

title: Immigration - ICE Encounter Rights
law_reference: Fourth Amendment; Immigration and Nationality Act
content: ICE agents need a judicial warrant signed by a judge to enter your home. An ICE administrative warrant (Form I-200 or I-205) does NOT give them the right to enter your home without consent. You can ask to see the warrant through a window or under the door before opening. You have the right to remain silent.
actionable_response: Do not open the door. Say: 'I do not consent to entry. Please show me a judicial warrant signed by a judge under the door.'

title: New York - Traffic Stop Rights
law_reference: New York Vehicle and Traffic Law § 375; People v. De Bour (1976)
content: In New York, during a traffic stop you must provide your driver's license, registration, and proof of insurance when requested. New York is NOT a stop-and-identify state, meaning you are not required to identify yourself if you are a pedestrian. However, in a vehicle, you must provide vehicle documents. You are not required to answer other questions.
actionable_response: Hand over license, registration, insurance. Then say: 'I prefer not to answer further questions without my attorney.'

title: New York - DWI Stop Rights
law_reference: New York Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1194; Implied Consent Law
content: New York has implied consent law — by driving you agree to a chemical test (breathalyzer/blood) if lawfully arrested for DWI. Refusing the test results in automatic license revocation for 1 year and a $500 fine, even if not convicted of DWI. Field sobriety tests are NOT mandatory — you can decline them without penalty.
actionable_response: You can decline field sobriety tests. Say: 'I decline the field sobriety test.' However, refusing a breathalyzer after arrest has consequences.

title: New York - Arrest Without Warrant
law_reference: New York Criminal Procedure Law § 140.10
content: In New York, police can arrest you without a warrant if they have probable cause to believe you committed a felony, or if they witness you committing any crime. You must be arraigned within 24 hours of arrest. You have the right to make a phone call after being booked. You cannot be held indefinitely without charges.
actionable_response: Stay calm. Say: 'Am I under arrest or am I free to go?' If arrested, say: 'I want a lawyer' and stop talking.

title: New York - Stop and Frisk Rules (Post-Floyd v. City of NY)
law_reference: Floyd v. City of New York, 959 F. Supp. 2d 540 (2013); CPL § 140.50
content: After the landmark Floyd ruling, NYPD officers must have reasonable suspicion of criminal activity to stop someone, not just a hunch. They must be able to articulate specific facts. Officers cannot stop someone based solely on race or neighborhood. If stopped, you can ask 'What is the reasonable suspicion for this stop?'
actionable_response: Ask calmly: 'Officer, what is your reasonable suspicion for stopping me?' Do not physically resist but verbally assert your rights.

title: California - Traffic Stop Rights
law_reference: California Vehicle Code § 12951; California Penal Code § 647(e)
content: In California, you must provide your driver's license, registration, and proof of insurance during a traffic stop. California is not a stop-and-identify state for pedestrians. You are not required to answer questions about where you are going or coming from. Passengers in a vehicle are generally not required to show ID unless suspected of a crime.
actionable_response: Provide vehicle documents. Say: 'I'm happy to provide my documents but I prefer not to answer questions without my attorney.'

title: California - Vehicle Search and Proposition 47
law_reference: California Penal Code § 1538.5; People v. Williams (1999)
content: In California, police need probable cause or a warrant to search your vehicle. Personal use amounts of some drugs are now misdemeanors under Prop 47, which may affect probable cause for searches. You can refuse consent to a search. If police search anyway, do not resist — the evidence may be suppressed in court.
actionable_response: Say clearly: 'I do not consent to this search.' Remain calm and do not physically resist.

title: California - Rights Upon Arrest
law_reference: California Penal Code § 825; California Penal Code § 851.5
content: In California, you must be brought before a magistrate within 48 hours of arrest (excluding weekends and holidays). You have the right to make at least 3 completed phone calls within 3 hours of arrest — one to an attorney, one to a bail bondsman, one to a relative. Police must allow these calls.
actionable_response: Say: 'I want my 3 phone calls as required by California law, and I want to speak to an attorney.' Stop answering questions.

title: California - Sanctuary State Protections
law_reference: California Values Act (SB 54); California Government Code § 7284
content: California is a sanctuary state. State and local law enforcement cannot use resources to enforce federal immigration law, detain people based solely on immigration detainer requests without a judicial warrant, or ask about immigration status during routine interactions. California residents have strong protections against local police cooperating with ICE.
actionable_response: You can say: 'Under California's Values Act, I am not required to answer questions about my immigration status.'

title: Texas - Traffic Stop and Stop-and-Identify Law
law_reference: Texas Transportation Code § 521.025; Texas Penal Code § 38.02
content: Texas IS a stop-and-identify state. If lawfully detained, you must provide your name, residence address, and date of birth upon request. Refusing to identify yourself when lawfully detained is a Class C misdemeanor. You must also provide driver's license, registration, and insurance during a traffic stop. You are not required to answer other questions.
actionable_response: Provide your name and vehicle documents. Say: 'I am providing my identification as required. I prefer not to answer further questions.'

title: Texas - Vehicle and Property Search
law_reference: Texas Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 18.01; Texas Constitution Art. 1 § 9
content: Texas law provides broader privacy protections than federal law in some cases. Police need probable cause or consent to search your vehicle. Texas courts have sometimes excluded evidence from searches based on state constitutional grounds. Never consent to a search. If police claim they smell marijuana, they may use this as probable cause.
actionable_response: Say: 'I do not consent to this search.' Repeat if asked again. Do not physically resist.

title: Texas - Arrest Rights and Magistration
law_reference: Texas Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 14.01, 15.17
content: In Texas, you must be taken before a magistrate within 48 hours of a warrantless arrest. The magistrate will inform you of your charges, set bail, and inform you of your rights including the right to counsel. You have the right to remain silent. Texas allows arrests for all fine-only offenses, including minor traffic violations.
actionable_response: Say: 'I am invoking my right to remain silent and I want an attorney.' Do not answer questions before speaking to a lawyer.

title: Florida - Traffic Stop and Stop-and-Identify
law_reference: Florida Statute § 322.15; Florida Statute § 856.021
content: Florida is a stop-and-identify state. If you are lawfully detained, you must identify yourself. During a traffic stop, you must provide your driver's license, registration, and proof of insurance. Florida has a 'Stop and Frisk' law that allows officers to temporarily detain and pat down someone if they have reasonable suspicion of criminal activity.
actionable_response: Provide your ID and vehicle documents. Say: 'I am providing ID as required. I do not consent to searches and prefer not to answer further questions.'

title: Florida - Search and Seizure Protections
law_reference: Florida Statute § 933.01; Article I, Section 12 of Florida Constitution
content: Florida's Constitution provides protection against unreasonable searches. Police need a warrant or valid exception (consent, plain view, incident to arrest, exigent circumstances) to search you. Florida courts have been active in protecting search rights. Never consent to a search as it waives your 4th Amendment protections.
actionable_response: Say: 'I do not consent to this search.' If asked why: 'I am simply exercising my constitutional right.'

title: Florida - First Appearance After Arrest
law_reference: Florida Rule of Criminal Procedure 3.130; Florida Statute § 907.041
content: In Florida, you must be brought before a judge within 24 hours of arrest for a first appearance hearing where bail conditions are set. You have the right to remain silent. Florida is a 'stand your ground' state, which may be relevant if self-defense is involved. You have the right to know the charges against you.
actionable_response: Say: 'I am invoking my right to remain silent and request an attorney.' Do not discuss the incident with anyone until you speak to a lawyer.

title: Am I Detained? - The Key Question
law_reference: Florida v. Bostick, 501 U.S. 429 (1991); United States v. Mendenhall (1980)
content: You have the right to ask police 'Am I being detained or am I free to go?' If you are not being detained, you can walk away. If they say you are detained, ask 'What is the reasonable suspicion for my detention?' Police must have articulable reasonable suspicion to detain you. A voluntary encounter can be ended by you at any time.
actionable_response: Ask calmly: 'Officer, am I being detained or am I free to go?' If free to go, calmly leave. If detained, ask for the reason.

title: Right to Record Police
law_reference: First Amendment; Glik v. Cunniffe, 655 F.3d 78 (1st Cir. 2011)
content: You have a First Amendment right to record police performing their duties in public. Police cannot order you to stop recording in a public space. They cannot seize your phone without a warrant. Do not physically obstruct police while recording. This right has been upheld in most federal circuits.
actionable_response: Say: 'I am exercising my First Amendment right to record.' Do not stop recording unless physically threatened. Back up footage to the cloud.

title: Excessive Force - Know Your Rights
law_reference: Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386 (1989); 42 U.S.C. § 1983
content: Police are only allowed to use force that is objectively reasonable under the circumstances. If police use excessive force, you can file a civil rights complaint under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. Do NOT physically resist even if the force seems excessive — resist only through legal channels. Document injuries immediately after.
actionable_response: Do not resist physically. Say clearly: 'I am not resisting.' Document everything afterward — photos, witnesses, badge numbers.
